subtitles.text: Welcome to this HACCP Level Two Training Programme,
specifically tailored for food and dairy professionals.
Today, we are going to explore the vital principles
of food safety management that keep our manufacturing processes
secure, compliant, and trusted by millions of consumers every
single day. Whether you work directly on the milk
intake deck, pasteurisation bays, cheese processing vats,
packing halls, or quality assurance,
this course will provide you with the practical knowledge
to protect our products, our brand,
and above all, our consumers.
Let's get started.

subtitles.text: Our primary aim today is twofold:
to summarise the HACCP system comprehensively and to review
how Critical Control Points function in our daily dairy
processing operations. Throughout this session,
we will cover the fundamental definition of HACCP,
the origins of the standard,
and the types of food hazards you might encounter
on site. We will examine key UK and European
regulations, break down the seven foundational principles of HACCP,
and discover exactly how Critical Control Points are determined
using structured decision trees.
We will also explore dairy-specific CCP examples,
monitoring routines, chemical, physical, biological,
and allergen controls, prerequisite programmes,
proper food safety attitude, corrective action plans via the
PDCA cycle, and your personal legal responsibilities.
We will then conclude with a knowledge assessment.

title: What is HACCP?
subtitle: Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point: built-in prevention at source

elements.heading: End-Product Inspection
elements.description:
• Testing finished product after manufacture
• High recall risk: unsafe product is already packaged
• Impossible to test 100% of manufactured units

subtitles.text: So, what exactly is HACCP?
HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point.
At its heart, it is an internationally recognised,
science-based food safety management system designed to do three
things: prevent, reduce, or eliminate hazards in food before
they ever reach a consumer.
Think about how traditional food quality used to work
decades ago—people relied heavily on testing finished products after
they were already made and packaged.
But end-product testing is like locking the stable door
after the horse has bolted.
HACCP completely shifts the focus:
it builds safety directly into every stage of the
production process. Under Codex Alimentarius guidelines,
HACCP operates on seven core principles,
starting from hazard analysis right through to record-keeping,
ensuring that potential issues are tackled proactively at source.

title: Where Does HACCP Come From?
subtitle: From 1960s NASA space missions to statutory international food legislation

elements.heading: NASA & Pillsbury
elements.description: Developed 100% safe, pathogen-free food for astronauts in zero gravity.

elements.heading: US FDA Adoption
elements.description: Formalised principles for commercial canning to stop botulism outbreaks.

elements.heading: Codex Standard
elements.description: FAO / WHO international benchmark adopted HACCP worldwide.

elements.heading: Mandatory UK Law
elements.description: Regulation (EC) 852/2004 makes HACCP compulsory for all food plants.

subtitles.text: You might be surprised to learn that HACCP was
originally born out of the space race!
In the 1960s, NASA collaborated with the U.S.
Army Laboratories and the Pillsbury Company to develop rations
for astronauts. In zero gravity,
a foodborne illness or even a few stray crumbs
could be fatal to a space mission.
They realised they needed a system that guaranteed one
hundred percent safety before the food left the launch
pad. In the 1970s, the U.S.
Food and Drug Administration adopted these principles for commercial
canned foods. By the 1990s,
the Codex Alimentarius Commission adopted HACCP internationally.
And in the 2000s, it became a strict legal
requirement across the UK and the European Union through
Regulation (EC) 852/2004.
What started as space technology is now the benchmark
of our daily dairy operations.

title: What Are the Hazards in Food?
subtitle: The four fundamental categories of food safety hazards in dairy processing

elements.heading: 1. Biological Hazards
elements.description: Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella, pathogenic E. coli and Bacillus cereus spores.

elements.heading: 2. Chemical Hazards
elements.description: Detergent residues, CIP chemicals, sanitisers, and machinery lubricants.

elements.heading: 3. Physical Hazards
elements.description: Glass fragments, brittle hard plastics, metal swarf, hair, screws, and pests.

elements.heading: 4. Allergen Hazards
elements.description: Unintended cross-contact with any of the 14 statutory recognized allergens.

subtitles.text: Let's define what we mean by a food hazard.
A food hazard is any biological,
chemical, or physical agent in food,
or condition of food, with the potential to cause
harm or make it unfit for human consumption.
As a dairy manufacturing business,
we are legally and ethically obligated to identify potential
hazards at every step of our process flow so
that they can be systematically eliminated or reduced to
safe levels. We classify food safety hazards into four
principal categories: First, Physical hazards—foreign objects such as metal
shavings, plastic, glass, or insects.
Second, Chemical hazards—such as cleaning chemical residues,
lubricants, or veterinary drug residues.
Third, Microbiological hazards—pathogenic bacteria like Listeria monocytogenes,
Salmonella, or E.
coli. And fourth, Allergen hazards—unintended cross-contact
with major recognised food allergens.

title: Regulations & Legal Framework
subtitle: Codex Alimentarius baseline, Regulation (EC) 852/2004 and EHO enforcement

elements.heading: Codex Alimentarius (FAO / WHO)
elements.description: Defines what hygiene rules are required internationally to protect global food trade.

elements.heading: Regulation (EC) No 852/2004
elements.description: Mandatory UK legislation requiring all food businesses to put in place a permanent HACCP system.

elements.heading: Environmental Health Officer (EHO) Powers
elements.description: EHOs inspect food plants regularly. Failure to maintain HACCP can result in immediate site closure, heavy statutory fines, and criminal prosecution.

subtitles.text: Food safety isn't just best practice—it is the law.
The foundational benchmark is the Codex Alimentarius,
established jointly by the Food and Agriculture Organisation and
the World Health Organisation.
Codex sets global baseline food hygiene standards to protect
consumer health and facilitate fair international trade.
A helpful way to think about this is:
Codex defines what the hygiene requirements are,
while HACCP provides the practical how-to framework to achieve
them in our dairy facility.
In the UK, this is made mandatory under Regulation
(EC) 852/2004. Environmental Health
Officers, or EHOs, inspect food facilities regularly.
If a food business fails to implement or maintain
an effective HACCP plan, the EHO possesses the statutory
power to issue heavy fines,
initiate criminal prosecution, or shut the facility down immediately.

title: The 7 Principles of HACCP
subtitle: The complete seven-step framework for dairy safety management

elements.heading: 1. Conduct Hazard Analysis
elements.description: Identify all biological, chemical, physical, and allergen risks across the process.

elements.heading: 2. Determine CCPs
elements.description: Identify steps essential to prevent, eliminate, or reduce hazards to safe levels.

elements.heading: 3. Establish Critical Limits
elements.description: Define clear pass/fail safety boundaries (e.g. >72°C / 15s in pasteurisation).

elements.heading: 4. Establish Monitoring
elements.description: Continuous real-time tracking and logging of all critical control parameters.

elements.heading: 5. Corrective Actions
elements.description: Pre-planned immediate procedures when monitoring shows a loss of control.

elements.heading: 6. Verification Procedures
elements.description: Audits, probe calibrations, and laboratory testing to confirm the system works.

elements.heading: 7. Documented Records
elements.description: Maintain robust documentation, trace logs, and due diligence compliance records.

subtitles.text: Let's walk through the Seven Principles of HACCP in
detail. Principle One: Conduct a Hazard Analysis.
We examine every single step in our dairy process
to identify biological, chemical, physical,
and allergen hazards.
Principle Two: Determine Critical Control Points,
or CCPs. These are the specific steps where a
control measure is essential to prevent,
eliminate, or reduce a hazard to an acceptable level.
Principle Three: Establish Critical Limits.
We define measurable boundaries—such as minimum pasteurisation temperatures and
holding times—that separate safe food from unsafe food.
Principle Four: Establish Monitoring Procedures.
We set up continuous or scheduled checks to confirm
that every CCP stays strictly within its critical limits.
Principle Five: Establish Corrective Actions.
If monitoring shows a deviation,
we execute immediate, predefined actions to regain control and
isolate non-compliant product.
Principle Six: Establish Verification Procedures.
Through audits, calibrations, and microbiological tests,
we verify that our HACCP system is working effectively.
And Principle Seven: Establish Record-Keeping.
We maintain clear, tamper-proof logs and documents proving our
safety controls have operated correctly.

title: Determining Critical Control Points
subtitle: Structured decision tree methodology to establish control points

elements.heading: Process Flow Diagram
elements.description: Construct an accurate flow diagram mapping every stage from raw milk intake to final shipping.

elements.heading: Hazard Analysis
elements.description: Evaluate the likelihood and severity of potential hazards at each step.

elements.heading: Codex Decision Tree
elements.description: Apply the 4 standard questions to determine if a step is a genuine CCP.

elements.heading: Establish Critical Limits
elements.description: Set validated, measurable parameters and operational monitoring procedures.

subtitles.text: Now let's focus on Principle Two:
Determining Critical Control Points.
A CCP is not just any control point in
the factory—it is a point,
step, or procedure where control can be applied,
and is completely essential to prevent or eliminate a
significant food safety hazard or reduce it to an
acceptable level. To determine CCPs accurately,
we follow a rigorous six-step method:
First, we map out a detailed processing flow of
the entire dairy line.
Second, we perform a thorough hazard analysis at every
single step. Third, we apply the standardised Codex CCP
Decision Tree. Fourth, we determine which steps qualify as
true Critical Control Points.
Fifth, we categorise the hazard by type of control—whether
microbiological, physical, chemical, or allergen.
And sixth, we establish strict critical limits and monitoring
routines for each.

title: Your Work Area CCPs
subtitle: Identifying and owning the Critical Control Points in your daily operational zone

elements.heading: Heat Treatment CCP
elements.description:
• Verify temperature (>72°C for 15s)
• Check automated divert valve response
• Inspect continuous chart records

elements.heading: Rapid Cooling CCP
elements.description:
• Pull down temperature to <8°C in 90 min
• Maintain cold store below <4°C target
• Prevent spore germination

elements.heading: Metal Detection CCP
elements.description:
• 100% finished pack inline inspection
• Hourly test piece validation (Fe/Non-Fe/SS)
• Auto-reject fail-safe mechanism

elements.heading: If in Doubt: Escalate Immediately
elements.description: Always notify your shift supervisor or QA manager if a parameter drifts.

subtitles.text: Take a brief moment to reflect on your daily
routine. Can you identify the specific Critical Control Points
in your immediate work area?
For instance, if you operate our milk pasteurisation plant,
do you know your exact critical temperature and divert
valve set points?
If you work in cheese packing or powdered dairy
lines, do you know the sensitivity limits of the
metal detector at the end of the line?
If you are ever unsure of how many CCPs
exist in your operational zone or what their critical
limits are, speak with your shift supervisor or quality
team immediately. Food safety starts with knowing your control
points inside out.

subtitles.text: Why is HACCP so vital to our dairy operations?
Here are eight fundamental reasons:
Number one: It helps us deeply understand all potential
food safety risks across our production lines.
Number two: It allows us to identify,
evaluate, and control hazards before they cause foodborne illness.
Number three: It puts robust preventive controls in place
at critical stages.
Number four: It protects consumer health,
preventing microbial infections and severe allergic reactions.
Number five: It maintains customer and retailer confidence in
the quality and safety of our dairy brand.
Number six: It safeguards our business reputation,
avoiding catastrophic product recalls.
Number seven: It provides clear guidance on statutory compliance.
And number eight: Quite simply,
we cannot legally trade or sell dairy products without
an active, validated HACCP system.

title: Production CCPs: Filtration & Heat Treatment
subtitle: Physical sediment removal and validated thermal pathogen kill steps

elements.heading: Raw Milk Filtration (1000 µm)
elements.description:
• In-line 1000-micron filter mesh at tanker intake
• Removes farm sediment, straw, and foreign particulate
• Filter integrity checked and logged before and after discharge

elements.heading: HTST Pasteurisation (>72°C / 15s)
elements.description:
• Thermal kill step for Listeria monocytogenes and Salmonella
• Automated flow divert valve triggers if temperature drops below 72.0°C
• Continuous temperature chart recording and hourly verification

elements.heading: Dessert & Curd Thermal Cook CCP (>86°C / 20 min)
elements.description: Validated thermal processing for dessert bases and cooked cheese recipes.

subtitles.text: Let's examine how CCPs work in practice within our
dairy processing facility.
First, consider Physical Hazard Control:
CCP One is our In-line Raw Milk Filtration and
Clarification system, equipped with fine filtration at one thousand
microns. This removes extraneous farm debris,
sediment, or particulate matter before raw milk enters processing.
Next, consider Pathogen Elimination through Thermal Processing:
CCP Two is our Continuous Milk Pasteuriser:
whole and skimmed milk must achieve a High-Temperature Short-Time
pasteurisation temperature greater than seventy-two degrees Celsius with a
validated holding time of at least fifteen seconds—or greater
than seventy-two degrees Celsius for two and a half
minutes in specialist dairy batch pasteurisers.
This thermal kill step destroys vegetative pathogens such as
Listeria, Salmonella, and E.
coli. For our thermal batch processing lines—such as cultured
dairy dessert bases and cheese curds—CCP Three enforces cooking
and heat treatment at greater than eighty-six degrees Celsius
for twenty minutes to achieve target microbiological reduction.

title: Production CCPs: Chilling & Metal Detection
subtitle: Spore germination inhibition and final packaging physical inspection

elements.heading: Rapid Chilling (<8°C in 90 min)
elements.description:
• Chills pasteurised milk and curds to <8.0°C within 90 minutes
• Target finished storage temperature below 4.0°C
• Inhibits germination of heat-resistant Bacillus cereus spores

elements.heading: In-Line Metal Detection
elements.description:
• 100% inspection of finished cheese, yogurt, and dessert packs
• Calibrated with Ferrous, Non-Ferrous, and Stainless Steel test pieces
• Automated reject mechanism diverts suspect packs to a locked bin

subtitles.text: Continuing with our operational CCPs:
To prevent microbiological regrowth, rapid chilling is essential.
Following thermal treatment, pasteurised dairy bases,
liquid creams, and fresh cheese curds must be chilled
below eight degrees Celsius—and ideally below four degrees Celsius—within
ninety minutes. Moving quickly through the temperature danger zone
prevents spore-forming bacteria such as Bacillus cereus from germinating
and multiplying. Finally, at the packaging end of our
lines, we control physical hazards with inline Metal Detectors.
CCP Four monitors our packed dairy lines—such as block
cheese, yogurt pots, and dairy desserts—checking for ferrous,
non-ferrous, and stainless steel contamination before products are boxed
and dispatched.

title: Monitoring Procedures & Deviation Management
subtitle: Live logging, automated divert valves, and environmental Listeria surveillance

elements.heading: Live Shift Logging
elements.description: Observations must match physical gauges. Never back-fill paperwork after the event.

elements.heading: Instant Fail-Safe Action
elements.description: If pasteuriser temp < 72°C, automated divert valve immediately diverts milk to balance tank.

elements.heading: Non-Conformance Reporting
elements.description: Raise an Incident Report immediately whenever a critical limit boundary is breached.

elements.heading: Listeria Surveillance
elements.description: Risk-based swabbing of plant drains, floors, and food contact surfaces.

subtitles.text: Principle Four requires effective monitoring.
In our dairy facility, we don't guess—we measure.
All CCP monitoring observations must match live production records
and provide immediate, accurate feedback.
If a temperature drops below a critical limit—for example,
if a pasteuriser temperature drops below seventy-two degrees—the automated
flow divert valve must trigger immediately,
and the operator must notify the Technical and Quality
team without delay.
A formal Non-Conformance and Incident Report must be raised
on the spot.
Alongside CCP monitoring, we conduct Environmental Monitoring.
This involves regular microbiological swab testing of surfaces,
drains, and air to verify Good Manufacturing Practices and
eradicate harborage sites for environmental pathogens like Listeria.
The frequency of testing is risk-based,
determined by the HACCP team's risk assessment.

title: Hazard Spotlight: Chemical Safety & CIP
subtitle: CIP sanitisation, Cleaning Instruction Cards (CICs), and prohibited tools

elements.heading: CIP & Sanitiser Control
elements.description: Use only company-approved chemicals at verified dilutions and contact times.

elements.heading: Cleaning Instruction Cards
elements.description: Follow CICs strictly: check chemical concentration, water temperature, and contact time.

elements.heading: Prohibited Cleaning Tools
elements.description: Sponges harbor bacteria. Wire scouring pads shed metal wires into dairy products. Both are banned on site.

subtitles.text: Let's look at Chemical Hazard management.
In a dairy plant, extensive Clean-In-Place (CIP) systems and
open plant sanitisation are carried out every day.
To avoid chemical contamination of our dairy products,
worktops, pipework, and equipment must only be cleaned using
chemicals from company-approved suppliers.
You must strictly follow the Cleaning Instruction Cards—known as
CICs. Ensure you use the exact chemical concentration,
correct water temperature, and required contact time,
using designated, approved cleaning tools.
Please take note: abrasive sponges and wire scouring pads
are strictly prohibited on site,
as they break apart and introduce both chemical and
physical hazards. Do you know who our approved chemical
suppliers are for your department?

title: Hazard Spotlight: Physical Safety
subtitle: Foreign body eradication, site glass policy, and emergency breakage procedures

elements.heading: Physical Contaminants
elements.description: Glass, brittle hard plastics, metal swarf, screws, nuts, jewellery, and hair.

elements.heading: Harm & Trauma
elements.description: Choking hazards, mouth lacerations, broken teeth, and internal punctures.

elements.heading: Strict Glass Ban
elements.description: Zero glass in production halls and staff canteens; daily perspex register audits.

elements.heading: Emergency Procedure
elements.description: Stop the line immediately, quarantine a 30m radius of product, and notify QA at once.

subtitles.text: Turning to Physical Hazards: a physical hazard is any
foreign object or extraneous matter that unintentionally enters food.
In the dairy sector, this includes glass fragments,
brittle plastics, metal swarf, hair,
personal items, loose screws, or insects.
Physical contaminants carry severe risks for consumers,
including choking, mouth lacerations, broken teeth,
and internal tissue damage.
To protect our products, glass is strictly forbidden in
staff canteens and processing halls.
If any glass, hard plastic,
or ceramic item is chipped or broken anywhere in
the production area, you must stop the line immediately,
quarantine all exposed product, and report the breakage to
your supervisor as part of our formal Glass and
Brittle Plastics Procedure.

subtitles.text: Allergen management is a life-or-death responsibility.
Under UK and EU law,
food businesses are legally required to declare the presence
of any of the fourteen major food allergens.
Let's run through all fourteen:
One: Celery—including stalks, leaves, seeds,
and celeriac. Two: Cereals containing gluten—such as wheat,
rye, barley, and oats.
Three: Crustaceans—such as crabs, prawns,
and lobster. Four: Eggs—found in baked items,
glazes, and dressings.
Five: Fish. Six: Lupin—used in specialist flours and
bakery products. Seven: Milk—the primary allergen in our dairy
operations, encompassing lactose, casein, whey,
butter, cheese, and cream.
Eight: Molluscs—including mussels and squid.
Nine: Mustard. Ten: Peanuts.
Eleven: Sesame Seeds.
Twelve: Soybeans—found in soy lecithin,
tofu, and sauces.
Thirteen: Sulphur dioxide and sulphites—used as preservatives.
And fourteen: Tree nuts—including almonds,
hazelnuts, walnuts, cashews, pecans,
Brazil nuts, pistachios, and macadamias.

title: Allergens on Our Dairy Site
subtitle: Managing allergen profiles across liquid milk, cheese, desserts, and yogurt lines

elements.heading: Milk & Dairy
elements.description: Present across all standard milk, cheese, cream, butter, and yogurt lines.

elements.heading: Gluten & Eggs
elements.description: Gluten in cheesecake crumb bases; Egg in chilled custards and baked puddings.

elements.heading: Soya & Sulphites
elements.description: Soya lecithin in chocolate coatings; Sulphites in fruit preparations and fruit syrups.

elements.heading: Clean-Down Protocol
elements.description: Full CIP wash and validated rapid protein swab testing between recipe changeovers.

subtitles.text: In our dairy processing facility,
Milk is our primary raw material and product allergen,
present across all our fresh milk,
butter, cheese, and yogurt lines.
However, when we produce flavoured yogurts,
desserts, or composite cheese blends,
additional allergens enter our facility.
For example: Cereals containing gluten are handled in our
layered dairy crumb pots; Egg is used in our
custard and baked dessert recipes;
Soy lecithin is present in chocolate dairy coatings;
and Sulphites may be found in dried fruit preparations
for yogurt toppings.
We must strictly segregate these ingredients to prevent allergen
cross-contact. Can you list all the allergens handled in
your specific production department?

title: Strict Nut-Free Site Facility Policy
subtitle: Mandatory zero-tolerance prohibition of peanuts, tree nuts, and sesame seeds

elements.heading: 100% Nut-Free Facility
elements.description:
• No Peanuts & Peanut Butter
• No Almonds, Hazelnuts, Walnuts
• No Cashews, Pecans, Pistachios
• No Brazil nuts & Macadamias
• No Sesame seeds & Sesame oils

elements.heading: Check Your Snacks & Meals
elements.description:
1. Check all personal snacks, cereal bars, chocolates, and bakery items.
2. Never bring prohibited nut items into staff canteens or lockers.
3. Applies strictly to all employees, agency staff, contractors, and visitors.
4. Report accidental introduction immediately to HR and QA.

subtitles.text: We operate a strict, zero-tolerance Nut-Free Site Policy.
Because tree nuts and peanuts can cause fatal anaphylactic
shock in vulnerable individuals, bringing any nuts onto this
site is strictly prohibited.
When you come to work,
your packed lunches and personal snacks must not contain
peanuts, almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, cashews,
pecans, Brazil nuts, pistachios, macadamias,
or sesame seeds.
This rule applies to everyone—permanent employees,
temporary workers, contractors, and visitors.
Always inspect your snack packaging before bringing food on
site.

title: Biological Safety & Dairy Microbial KPIs
subtitle: Batch release criteria and laboratory microbiological release limits

subtitles.text: Let's explore Biological Hazards and our Key Performance Indicators
for dairy products—including pasteurised milk,
cream, cheese, and yogurt bases.
We test every production batch against strict microbiological specifications:
For Total Viable Count—or TVC—our target is less than
five thousand colony-forming units per gram,
with an absolute rejection threshold at ten thousand.
For Presumptive Enterobacteriaceae—our hygiene indicator—the target is less
than twenty per gram, and anything at twenty or
above is rejected.
For Presumptive Staphylococcus aureus, our target is less than
twenty per gram, rejected at twenty or above.
For Salmonella species, the standard is absolute:
Absent in twenty-five grams.
Any presence triggers an immediate batch rejection and investigation.
For Listeria monocytogenes, the standard is equally strict:
Absent in twenty-five grams.
And for Presumptive Bacillus cereus,
our target is less than one hundred per gram,
with rejection at greater than five hundred per gram.
Can you name the top three pathogens we work
hardest to exclude from dairy environments?

title: Personal Hygiene & 20-Second Handwashing
subtitle: The primary frontline defence protecting open dairy products from contamination

elements.heading: Wet Hands & Apply Soap
elements.description: Use clean running warm water and approved antibacterial foam soap.

elements.heading: Scrub for 20 Seconds
elements.description: Thoroughly scrub palms, backs of hands, between fingers, thumbs, and wrists.

elements.heading: Complete Rinse
elements.description: Rinse completely under running warm water to remove all soap residue.

elements.heading: Dry & Sanitise
elements.description: Dry with single-use paper towels and apply alcohol hand rub.

subtitles.text: Personal hygiene is our frontline defence against product contamination.
Even the most sophisticated pasteuriser cannot compensate for poor
operator hygiene. Handwashing is mandatory before entering production,
after using the toilet, after touching waste or non-sanitised
surfaces, and whenever changing tasks or handling allergens.
Use warm water and anti-bacterial soap,
scrubbing thoroughly across your palms,
backs of hands, between fingers,
thumbs, and wrists for at least twenty seconds.
Rinse completely and dry using single-use paper towels or
approved air dryers.
Remember: clean hands save lives.

title: Factory Hygiene Zoning & Stationery Coding
subtitle: Strict barrier controls between raw intake, intermediate processing, and packing halls

elements.heading: Green Pen & Stationery
elements.description: Open ready-to-eat filling hall. Full captive white boots, overcoats, and positive air pressure.

elements.heading: Red Pen & Stationery
elements.description: Pasteurised cheese curds and yogurt processing vats. Footwear barrier and captive utensils.

elements.heading: Blue Pen & Stationery
elements.description: Raw tanker intake deck, chemical store, outer packaging warehouse, and general corridors.

subtitles.text: To prevent cross-contamination, our dairy plant is divided into
distinct hygiene zones: Low-Risk, High-Care,
and High-Risk areas.
All packaging, ingredients, and utensils must be sanitised before
entering High-Care and High-Risk rooms.
Personal mobile phones are permitted for authorised personnel only
and MUST be thoroughly sanitised at the hygiene airlock
before entry. For tablets, pens,
clipboards, and electrical equipment that cannot be immersed in
water, use approved sanitising wipes.
We also maintain a strict pen colour-coding system:
Green Pens are used exclusively in High-Risk areas;
Red Pens are used exclusively in High-Care areas;
and Blue Pens are used exclusively in Low-Risk areas.
Never carry stationery or tools between zones without decontaminating
them.

title: Prerequisite Programmes (PRPs)
subtitle: The 7 structural pillars supporting the entire dairy HACCP food safety framework

elements.heading: Cleaning & CIP
elements.description: Automated CIP cycles and titration logs.

elements.heading: Hygiene & PPE
elements.description: Handwashing, hairnets, and illness reporting.

elements.heading: Pest Control
elements.description: Bait boxes, fly killers, and contractor audits.

elements.heading: Maintenance
elements.description: PPM servicing and food-grade lubricants.

elements.heading: Suppliers
elements.description: BRCGS certified ingredients & raw milk tests.

elements.heading: Allergens
elements.description: Dedicated equipment and clean-down checks.

elements.heading: Training
elements.description: Competence assessments and refreshers.

subtitles.text: Before a HACCP plan can succeed,
the manufacturing facility must have strong Prerequisite Programmes—or PRPs.
PRPs are the foundational environmental and operational hygiene conditions
necessary for producing safe food.
They manage general baseline hazards so that our HACCP
team can focus on specific Critical Control Points.
There are seven key PRP pillars:
One: Cleaning and Sanitation—routine CIP and deep-cleaning schedules.
Two: Personal Hygiene—clothing standards, health monitoring,
and hairnets. Three: Pest Control—professional baiting,
monitoring, and insect screens.
Four: Equipment and Premises Maintenance—preventive engineering routines.
Five: Supplier Control—auditing and approving dairy farms and ingredient
vendors. Six: Allergen Management—strict segregation and scheduling.
And Seven: Staff Training—ensuring every colleague understands food safety.

title: Cross-Contamination & 4-Point Labelling
subtitle: Segregation rules and the mandatory open ingredient container labelling system

elements.heading: Storage & Tool Separation
elements.description:
• Separate raw milk from pasteurised products
• Store all ingredients in sealed, dedicated tubs
• Never place ingredient containers directly on the floor
• Use designated colour-coded scoops for each recipe

elements.heading: 4-Point Container Label
elements.description:
1. Ingredient Name & Batch Code
2. Date Opened / Thawed
3. Secondary Use-By Date (e.g. 72h max)
4. Operator Signature / ID Number

subtitles.text: Safety isn't just a manual on a shelf—it's a
mindset and an attitude we bring to work every
shift. To prevent cross-contamination, keep raw milk and processed
dairy strictly segregated.
Use dedicated colour-coded utensils, buckets,
and valves. Always clean and sanitise equipment between recipes,
especially when switching to allergen-free lines.
In storage, keep all ingredients in sealed containers.
Every container MUST have an intact label showing four
pieces of information: First, the Ingredient Name;
Second, the Date Opened or Thawed;
Third, the Use-By Date; and Fourth,
the Operator's Name.
If an ingredient lacks a clear label,
do not use it.
Report it immediately.

title: Corrective Actions & The PDCA Quality Cycle
subtitle: Regaining control, investigating root causes, and standardising permanent fixes

elements.heading: 1. PLAN
elements.description:
• Define hazard analysis
• Set critical limits & tolerances
• Prepare SOPs and CIC cards

elements.heading: 2. DO
elements.description:
• Execute HACCP procedures
• Monitor CCPs in real-time
• Log data accurately on shift

elements.heading: 3. CHECK
elements.description:
• Audit shift records
• Calibrate thermometers
• Review lab microbiology reports

elements.heading: 4. ACT
elements.description:
• Investigate deviations
• Standardise corrective fixes
• Update the HACCP plan

subtitles.text: What happens when something goes wrong?
That is where Corrective Actions come into play.
A corrective action is a specific procedure taken when
monitoring shows that a CCP has deviated from its
critical limit. It has three aims:
bring the process back under control,
determine the root cause, and prevent recurrence.
For example, if a pasteuriser temperature drops below seventy-two
degrees Celsius, the diverter automatically returns the milk to
the balance tank.
The operator logs the incident,
quarantines any suspect product, and investigates the steam supply
or heat exchanger.
We utilise the PDCA quality cycle to continuously refine
our HACCP plan: Plan: Conduct hazard analyses and set
critical limits. Do: Implement controls,
train teams, and execute routines.
Check: Monitor CCPs, review thermograph charts,
and run audits.
Act: Standardise fixes, update procedures,
and prevent repeat deviations.

title: The HACCP Team & Individual Legal Liability
subtitle: Multidisciplinary ownership, quarantine protocols, and personal statutory responsibility

elements.heading: Multidisciplinary Team
elements.description: Operations, Quality Assurance, Engineering, Hygiene, and Warehousing working collaboratively.

elements.heading: ON-HOLD Protocol
elements.description: Attach physical Yellow/Red ON-HOLD tag immediately and lock batch in ERP. Only QA can release quarantined lots.

elements.heading: Personal Legal Liability
elements.description: Under Regulation (EC) 852/2004, individuals can be held personally liable for falsifying records or concealing safety breaches.

subtitles.text: Developing and maintaining HACCP requires teamwork.
A HACCP Team is a multidisciplinary group comprising operations,
quality assurance, engineering, and hygiene specialists.
Whenever an out-of-specification event occurs,
immediate action is required: place the affected product ON-HOLD
with physical quarantine tags.
The Technical and Quality team will investigate and determine
whether the product can be safely reprocessed or must
be destroyed. Remember: Food safety is not just the
Quality department's job—it is a shared responsibility across every
single team member.
Under UK food law, any individual employee who knowingly
breaches hygiene regulations or falsifies records can be held
personally legally accountable for foodborne illness outbreaks.
Let us take pride in keeping our dairy products
safe and our reputation uncompromised.
